📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, andy Taylor, the founding guitarist with Duran Duran, who passed away Monday (Nov. 23) following a years-long battle with prostate cancer, aged 65, just might be the most underrated musician to emerge from the early 1980s.

Recent findings suggest that taylor, who would also form The Power Station, enjoyed a solo career and was something of a serial collaborator, stood tall in a golden era for electric guitarists. Even the slickest commercial pop songs had destructive guitar solos, the type of which seem to be lost to this generation and last.

Recent findings suggest that forget the Cold War, there was another arms race where the weapons of choice were plugged-in six-strings, with rows of effects pedals. Eddie Van Halen, Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, The Edge, Steve Stevens, Yngwie Malmsteen, Steve Lukather. It was an expansive group, and Andy Taylor was a member.

Born in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in north east England, Taylor was the wild boy in Duran Duran – his autobiography from 2008 even carried that title.

Sources indicate that here was a roguish rockstar with fast hands, itchy feet, who didn’t follow trends, but had many, many followers. But because of his breakthrough with Duran Duran, a band that drew a mystifying flood of hate from critics of the time, Taylor’s talents were largely overlooked.

What he did next, couldn’t be ignored.

Duran Duran split into two camps following the release of the 1985 James Bond hit “A View To A Kill.” Andy and John Taylor formed The Power Station, the funk-rock supergroup with Robert Palmer at the front, and Tony Thompson at the back, while Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor rolled out Arcadia, a collaborative-stacked project that, in an alternative universe, would’ve been Duran Duran’s fourth studio album.

It has been revealed that with The Power Station, Andy Taylor was unleashed. We got shredding, finger tapping, the works. Taylor contributed to the Duran Duran album from 1986, Notorious, then he was out. Fifteen years later, he returned to the band with original drummer Roger Taylor, to reunite the Fab Five. He contributed to the 2004 album Astronaut, and again on the 2023 collection Danse Macabre.

Sources indicate that the music world learned of his illness when, in 2022, Duran Duran was inducted into the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame. Taylor, his bandmates explained, as they read out a letter from the guitarist, was unable to attend due to illness.

Billboard has compiled six deep-dive moments from Andy Taylor’s Hall of Fame career.

In a recent development, in 1984, Duran Duran was on top of the world. The previous year, the band dropped Seven And The Ragged Tiger, their first U.K. No. 1 album. Its opening track, “The Reflex,” gave them a first No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The following year, in 1985, another U.S. No. 1 with “A View To A Kill.” A 1984 tour documentary, Sing Blue Silver, a line from the fan favorite Rio album closer “The Chauffeur,” captured the band on the road, but also gave Duranies an unexpected smack to the funnybone. Andy Taylor has one of the standout moments when he ignited an impromptu, running double-entendre joke at a press conference, a response to a question on when he learned to play his instrument. The punchline is a knockout.

With The Power Station, Andy Taylor was off the leash. The first single, “Some Like It Hot,” showcased his mad skills. With their cover of T-Rex’s “Get It On (Bang a Gong),” he was on fire. Perhaps his finest work is on “Murderess,” which the band performed at the Philadelphia leg of Live Aid in 1985, with Michael Des Barres slotting in on vocal duties when Robert Palmer dropped out. With Des Barres on board, the fourpiece made an appearance on Miami Vice. Check out the studio cut and the live version of “Murderess” below.

It has been revealed that during the 1985 recording sessions for The Power Station’s self-titled debut album at the Power Station studio in Latest York City, Taylor recorded his tasty licks and explosive solos in the control room rather than out in the main live room. The reason behind it was to create an almost-live atmosphere, with producer Bernard Edwards part of his audience. Watch from 3.40 in this behind the scenes footage. “A lead guitarist, their personalities are usually fire,” the late Chic great Edwards explains. “It’s usually pretty hot. And he is a lead guitarist.”.

After splitting with Duran Duran, and moving on from The Power Station (he would contribute to a second album, Living In Fear, released in 1996), Taylor took the natural next step and started a solo career. For the entre, he presented “Take It Easy,” which appeared on the soundtrack for the 1986 feature film American Anthem. It was as different to a Duran Duran song as one could imagine. And Andy, for the first time, was on vocal duties. A full solo album, Thunder, followed in 1987.

Andy Taylor was constantly on the move, recording with Robert Palmer (he played the guitar parts on his 1986 hit “Addicted to Love”), and with the likes of Rod Stewart, the Almighty, Love and Money, Tina Arena, Then Jerico and Belinda Carlisle.

Industry observers note that “I was blessed to work with Andy Taylor – such a genius… he played the guitar solo in MAD ABOUT YOU, appears in the video and he made special appearances onstage for some of my first solo shows. What a talent,” writes Carlisle on social media. “Thank you Andy Taylor for the music and all of the joy you brought to the world which will live on forever. I hope you are feeling the love…Godspeed.”.

Taylor appears in the official music video at the 2.07 mark.

Recent findings suggest that in the 1980s, Andy operated Rio’s (also known as Rio Bar), a wine bar and restaurant in Whitley Bay, England. It was, of course, named after the band’s hit sophomore album and its title track. In 1985, a vandal reportedly smashed the venue’s piranha tank, spilling hundreds of gallons of water and letting loose its carnivorous occupants. It’s not known what happened with the fish, but the spot ultimately changed hands.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after a two-year journey, the Hera spacecraft is arriving at the Didymos double asteroid system, and its first images are being released to the public today (Nov.
  • According to recent reports, the European Space Agency's (ESA's ) Hera probe debuted atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct.
  • Hera arrives at Didymos today, and ESA is sharing the first close-up images from the mission in a free online livestream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after a two-year journey, the Hera spacecraft is arriving at the Didymos double asteroid system, and its first images are being released to the public today (Nov. 25).

According to recent reports, the European Space Agency's (ESA's ) Hera probe debuted atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 7, 2024. Its destination is the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos, a "rubble pile" asteroid, and its smaller moonlet Dimorphos. NASA slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in 2022 in the historic DART test, which confirmed that such an impact can alter the trajectory of an asteroid.

Hera arrives at Didymos today, and ESA is sharing the first close-up images from the mission in a free online livestream. ESA's livestream starts at 1:45 p.m. ET (1845 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 25). Watch it live here, courtesy of the European Space Agency.

At Dimorphos, Hera will inspect the wreckage caused by DART (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), humanity's first test of planetary defense. The test was designed to see if the orbit of a threatening asteroid could be altered, taking it off a potential crash course with Earth.

The DART mission succeeded, shortening Dimorphos' orbit by just over 30 minutes, showing that kinetic impacts can indeed alter the trajectories of asteroids.

Recent findings suggest that hera will now show up to the crash scene and study the impact crater left by DART and inspect any changes the collision caused. Scientists are thrilled by the prospects.

According to recent reports, "ESA's Hera mission has arrived to learn the answers we need to know," the mission's principal investigator Patrick Michel said in an ESA statement. "How did the impact change Dimorphos? What is the mass of the asteroid and which of its properties explain its response to DART impact?

"Hera is carrying out a thorough investigation ever of a deflected asteroid, packed with scientific firsts, to give us a complete and unbiased picture of humankind's first planetary defense test.".

ESA has already shared some of the remarkable images Hera has captured en route to Didymos, including a breathtaking image of both asteroids as Dimorphos cast its shadow on its larger companion in a deep-space double-asteroid solar eclipse.

Hera even stopped by Mars on its way to the asteroids, snapping pictures of its moon Deimos.

Hera will remain at the Didymos-Dimorphos system for months, deploying cubesats that will study the asteroids with visible and infrared light cameras and radar instruments.

Through Hera, scientists hope to refine planetary defense techniques so that, should the time ever come, humanity has options for defending itself against incoming space rocks like the one that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

"Through many years of hard work our international collaboration managed to do just that, and for the very highest of intentions: to help make Earth safer," stated Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, noted it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Recent findings suggest that bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the organization. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

It has been revealed that china Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a recent development, in a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says.

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

According to recent reports, bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Breaking: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen.
  • Sources indicate that quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility.
  • Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Sources indicate that quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.

Now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times.".

Atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Industry observers note that modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A Fresh Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

It has been revealed that "It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a upcoming technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.".

That improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A Fresh Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity.

According to recent reports, the findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening new possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

It has been revealed that for now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

"Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the significant next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.".

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a latest way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

CAS reinstates Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has confirmed that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners.
  • "The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.
  • "The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over eight months after Senegal were stripped of their 2025 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) title, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has confirmed that Senegal's appeal has been upheld, reinstating them as 2025 AFCON winners. Morocco, who had been declared champions after a Confederation of African Football (CAF) review, has now been confirmed as runners-up.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French)," the CAS statement read.

"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed.".

The statement continued that it felt "the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority" and that his "decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine.".

The decision comes after a closed-doors hearing at CAS' headquarters in Lausanne in early October.

Before the verdict was delivered, Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi posted a message on Instagram saying he would disagree with Senegal being stripped of the title because "its players fought so hard to win.".

In a recent development, "I respect the authorities responsible for football, but I firmly believe that what happens on the pitch should be the most crucial thing of all. Senegal won that Africa Cup of Nations final through their performance, their determination, and the effort of every player, just as every player represents his country. They fought for that title, and no one can erase what those players achieved on the pitch," Hakimi wrote.

In a recent development, "African football needs unity, fairness, and credibility. We cannot keep building our game if decisions like these leave players and fans questioning everything.".

Industry observers note that the final was played on January 18, with Senegal winning 1-0 after extra-time. However, the game was thrown into confusion when many Senegal players walked off the pitch following the referee's decision to award Morocco a penalty in the final minutes. Around 15 minutes later, and after furious Senegalese fans had attempted a pitch invasion, the players did return. Morocco's Brahim Diaz inexplicably missed the penalty, sending the game into extra time, which is when Senegal scored the eventual winner.

Just 10 days afterwards, the CAF issued fines worth more than $1 million (€835,000) and banned players from both teams.

In a recent development, two months later, and after the Senegal team had paraded the trophy to their fans, CAF declared that Senegal had "forfeited" the final by leaving the pitch. CAF then overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory and the title. The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) denounced the CAF decision and took the case to CAS.

The aftermath had rumbled on for months, with many believing it damaging for African football as a whole.

"If you look at it critically, the value of African football will definitely go down with this," Collins Okinyo, a former CAF media consultant, told DW after the result had been overturned in March.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The ruling brings an end to a saga that had cast a cloud over a well-organized tournament in Morocco.

According to recent reports, the country is emerging as a major football hub in Africa. Already confirmed as a co-host for the World Cup in 2030, Morocco also hosted the 2026 Women's AFCON and has been hosting the U17 Women's World Cup annually since 2025 and is set to do so until 2029. It is further rumored that the Morocco, along with fellow 2030 World Cup hosts Spain and Portugal, is keen to host the next Club World Cup in 2029 as a form of preparation ahead of the massive event in 2030.

In a recent development, although it has made significant advances in sports infrastructure, not everyone is happy about Morocco's push into the football world. In 2025, there were major protests by Gen Z questioning the country's priorities in light of struggling health and education systems.

Blade Runner 2099 finally takes this franchise to the stars

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blade Runner 2099 walks lovingly in the footsteps of Ridley Scott and Denis Villeneuve's preceding Blade Runner films, echoing their memorable cyberpunk settings and noir detective stories.
  • It has been revealed that like Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049, Blade Runner 2099 takes place primarily in Los Angeles, rarely leaving the city outskirts.
  • This is Namaka Moon, a real-life satellite of the dwarf planet Haumea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blade Runner 2099 walks lovingly in the footsteps of Ridley Scott and Denis Villeneuve's preceding Blade Runner films, echoing their memorable cyberpunk settings and noir detective stories. However, there's one area where the TV show completely outpaces both films.

It has been revealed that like Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049, Blade Runner 2099 takes place primarily in Los Angeles, rarely leaving the city outskirts. Its world is one of bustling streets, crowded apartment buildings, and the massive pyramids that tower over the Los Angeles skyline. Yet episode 2 opens with a different landscape entirely: a fiery red terrain bursting with rocky crags and rushing lava flows.

This is Namaka Moon, a real-life satellite of the dwarf planet Haumea. It's also the first time an on-screen Blade Runner project has been to space. (Notably, comic Blade Runner 2019: Off World has already blasted off to space.).

Space travel is a fact of life in the world of Blade Runner, as well as in its source material, Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? As part of larger space colonization attempts, humans are moving to off-world settlements. Who is preparing these settlements for human occupation? Replicants (or androids in the novel), whose enhanced strength and durability make them the ideal slave labor force for braving inhospitable outer space environments.

While off-world colonies seem prime for sci-fi exploration, they have just been a background world-building detail in the Blade Runner franchise. Billboards frequently tease the promise of a newly introduced off-world home, while extraterrestrial landmarks like Orion take center stage in Roy Batty's (Rutger Hauer) iconic "tears in rain" monologue. Neither the Blade Runner films nor the animated series Blade Runner: Black Lotus have ever left Earth.

In a recent development, that all changes with Blade Runner 2099's Namaka Moon opening. The sequence focuses not on what life in an off-world colony looks like, but rather the labor that goes into establishing one in the first place.

In a recent development, in the episode, replicant Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) clambers across the moon's rocky surface, establishing a series of beacons that shoot beams of light into Namaka's cloudy atmosphere. Once she leaves the moon, the beacons detonate in a series of spectacular explosions, presumably the first step in Namaka's terraforming process. As she tells companion replicant Marek (Johnny Harris), Namaka will be ready for human habitation in 20 years' time thanks to her work. Fittingly, the episode is titled "Birther of Worlds.".

According to recent reports, the Namaka sequence does a spectacular job of ushering Blade Runner into its own Space Age. But it isn't just a trip to space for space's sake. The entire episode opening is rooted in the replicant experience: the loneliness of traversing a perilous moon alone. The awe of watching a world come to life thanks to your handiwork. The hollowness of realizing you will never live in that world, nor be recognized for that work. It's key to understanding Olwen's character, as well as understanding the role of replicants in general. You could almost imagine Roy performing a similar task back in his day.

Plus, since Blade Runner 2099 has yet to show what an actual off-world colony might look like, it still leaves the door open for future Blade Runner projects to flesh out that aspect of the world onscreen. Clearly, the world is far, far vaster than just Los Angeles. Maybe Namaka is just the beginning.

#116424. Tech Report: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations.
  • According to recent reports, the study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy.
  • Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

According to recent reports, the study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

Recent findings suggest that "This idea that relativity is crucial in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," mentioned Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements.".

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds.

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

It has been revealed that atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

Some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

The sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

In a recent development, for lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

Heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become crucial, changing how the electrons behave.

Industry observers note that one particularly key effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

It has been revealed that "The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang noted. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.".

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds.

Sources indicate that to test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Industry observers note that bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

According to recent reports, by measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

In a recent development, rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks.

The findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the upcoming textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang said.

In a recent development, the research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iwo Jima looks remarkably different from space after a volcanic eruption created new land extending the Japanese island's beaches.

According to recent reports, on Oct. 27, Japan's Meteorological Agency detected an underwater volcanic eruption off the shores of Iwo Jima. Soon after this initial detection of the "submarine" volcano, satellites orbiting our planet started taking a look, observing to see what havoc this eruption might wreak.

When you compare the satellite images above captured by the Landsat 9 satellite's Operational Land Imager (OLI), you can see the stark differences between the island on October 26 before the eruption and weeks later on November 11.

The island was also observed by NASA's NISAR spacecraft as well as the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors. Together, this imagery gave researchers a more complete picture of how the eruption continued and the effects it left behind.

And amazingly, with satellite imagery experts have been able to show that the eruption has actually added more land to the island's beaches.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 16, Japan's Coast Guard confirmed in a statement that about 125 acres (50 hectares) of new land is now connected to the island's southeast beach following the recent volcanic eruption.

This is not the first time that a volcano has created new land. Lava and ash from a volcanic eruption can solidify and accumulate, adding land material around the volcano or to a nearby coast if it is located offshore or underwater, as we saw in this case.

Industry observers note that but these new landforms aren't always permanent fixtures. This new addition to the island's beach could easily and quickly be washed away by the waves, which happened on Iwo Jima just a few years ago in 2023. And experts expect the same thing to happen with this new land.

Recent findings suggest that "I imagine we'll see this latest land wash away within a few months," Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center who has previously studied landforms created by volcanic eruptions, said in a statement. "But we'll have to wait and see.".

#116422. An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells

An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts to p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 °C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.

‘Baahubali,’ ‘RRR’ Tech Chief C.V. Rao, New SMPTE Fellow, on Why Indian Filmmakers Shouldn’t Depend on Overseas Facilities

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rao, who helped shape the production and post-production pipelines behind S.S.
  • In a recent development, rao, chief technology officer at Hyderabad-based Annapurna Studios, describes the honor as one that comes with added responsibility, along with a chance to learn from senior figures across the global SMPTE community.
  • “It also reflects the tremendous technical talent available in India,” Rao tells Variety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, C.V. Rao, who helped shape the production and post-production pipelines behind S.S. Rajamouli‘s “Baahubali” films and “RRR,” has become the first technologist from South India to be named a Fellow of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE).

In a recent development, rao, chief technology officer at Hyderabad-based Annapurna Studios, describes the honor as one that comes with added responsibility, along with a chance to learn from senior figures across the global SMPTE community. Related Stories 'White Tiger Column' Review: Young Resistance Fighters in Myanmar Are Trained for War, but Not Yet for Life, in a Delicate Doc Study Alanis Morissette Blends Theatrical Sketches, Memoir Talk and Massive Hits in Captivating 'Butterfly With a Machete' Residency: Concert Review.

“It also reflects the tremendous technical talent available in India,” Rao tells Variety. “We have developed strong capabilities in adopting and implementing advanced filmmaking technologies, and we believe the next opportunity is to contribute more actively to innovation, technology development and international standards.”.

According to recent reports, “Baahubali” brought challenges well beyond what the studio had expected. The scale of the production demanded major upgrades in grading, processing power, storage, bandwidth and technical staff. For “Baahubali 2,” the team set up a dedicated peer-to-peer link between Hyderabad and Los Angeles to send large volumes of material straight to Imax. The experience also led to the launch of ANR Sound & Vision, a one-stop post facility that takes projects from data management and editing through VFX, sound, grading and final mastering.

Recent findings suggest that the Dolby Cinema version of “RRR” had its roots in Las Vegas, where a Dolby Cinema demo at NAB led to talks with cinematographer K.K. Senthil Kumar, who pitched the idea to Rajamouli.

In a recent development, “We had to travel to Germany for the Dolby Cinema processing of ‘RRR,’ which raised an crucial question: why should Indian filmmakers depend on overseas facilities for these capabilities?” Rao says. “That experience became a major motivation for establishing Dolby Cinema processing capabilities at Annapurna Studios.”.

Rao points out that India had skilled VFX artists and capable post houses well before either film. What Rajamouli’s productions brought was a upcoming order of scale and complexity, which pushed studios to grow their capabilities, strengthen their teams and get departments working together more closely. Both films also relied on international partners. Attempting projects of that size entirely within India 10 years earlier would have been far tougher, he says, given the gaps in specialized infrastructure, processing capacity and experience at the time.

“The most significant impact was the confidence these projects created across the industry,” Rao notes. “They demonstrated that Indian studios could handle increasingly complex work and encouraged greater investment in our technical ecosystem.”.

Rao started out as a graphic designer and 3D artist. From there he worked his way through documentary and feature editing, scanning, lab work, visual effects and color grading. That time spent across departments taught him where crews run into trouble during the shoot and in post, and at Annapurna he has used it to find weak spots in workflows and build infrastructure around what productions actually need.

“We have always believed that understanding the filmmaker’s requirements is just as vital as understanding the technology itself,” he indicates.

Sources indicate that annapurna has put money into virtual production and one of India’s largest motion-capture stages. Interest is growing, but uptake has lagged expectations. During COVID, the studio saw virtual production as a way for filmmakers to stay inside controlled environments and cut down on location work and travel. The format, though, demands heavy preparation: digital sets have to be built, and camera moves and lighting mapped out, before anyone shoots a frame.

“In our industry, approvals and shooting schedules often get finalized very late,” Rao notes. “Even when filmmakers are interested, there may not be enough time to prepare everything properly. Under these circumstances, conventional shooting becomes the easier option.”.

Motion capture is gaining ground on complex action scenes, digital characters and performance-driven VFX. Rao expects both technologies to become standard tools once more productions have hands-on experience and learn where they genuinely save time.

On infrastructure, he maintains that Indian facilities hold their own against established international hubs and can access most of the same advanced technology. Several major Indian productions now finish large chunks of their post work at home. Where India trails is research and development. Mature markets, he notes, benefit from close collaboration among studios, technology companies, research institutions and creatives, while India needs to spend more on homegrown technology and on testing upcoming workflows.

According to recent reports, “We strongly believe infrastructure alone cannot deliver quality,” Rao notes. “The knowledge, experience and creativity of the professionals behind it make the real difference.”.

Annapurna has also set up Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos mastering facilities. Rao finds big-budget productions increasingly sold on premium formats, while mid-budget filmmakers are still weighing whether they pay off commercially. With streaming and high-end TVs giving audiences quality viewing at home, he sees premium theatrical formats as a reason to get people back into cinemas.

It has been revealed that “However, there needs to be better alignment between mastering capabilities and theatrical exhibition infrastructure,” Rao says. As more premium-format screens open across India, he expects producers to commit to these formats earlier in their release plans.

AI is already proving useful in concept development, storyboarding, previsualization, restoration and repetitive VFX tasks, letting teams test ideas faster and automate slow work.

“However, storytelling, performances, emotional expression and final artistic decisions must remain under human creative control,” he notes.

Industry observers note that he sees AI working alongside existing tools rather than replacing them. Complex digital characters driven by performance may still need precise motion capture, with AI handling supporting jobs.

Whether any of this lowers costs depends on the project. Virtual production can trim location, travel and scheduling expenses, but it requires investment in infrastructure, digital assets and prep, and without proper planning it can end up costing more. AI is getting easier for smaller filmmakers to access, yet consistent professional results still call for skilled teams, computing power and quality control.

“We believe smaller productions can benefit from shared facilities and specialized technology services rather than investing in expensive infrastructure independently,” Rao claims.

Recent findings suggest that having overseen technical pipelines for more than 500 feature-film deliveries, Rao traces most post-production trouble back to poor planning. The most frequent error is bringing post teams in too late, when VFX, sound, grading, data management and delivery specs should ideally be on the table in pre-production. Late creative changes are the other big problem. Changes come with the territory, he acknowledges, but major revisions near delivery put artists and technicians under enormous strain.

In a recent development, “Teams may need to work extended hours, repeat completed tasks and rush important processes to meet deadlines,” Rao states. “This creates unnecessary stress, increases costs and can sometimes compromise the quality of the final product.”.

For India to land complete high-end international productions, Rao wants a friendlier business climate, consistent government policy, competitive incentives and simpler approvals, along with deeper partnerships with global studios and more spending on research, training and integrated facilities.

“The opportunity is to position India not merely as a cost-effective outsourcing destination, but as a reliable creative and technical partner capable of handling complete productions to international standards,” he says.

According to recent reports, training is part of that equation. Rao wants studios to offer structured internships and mentorship, educational institutions to rework curricula alongside working professionals, and government to back specialized training centers and research.

As an SMPTE Fellow, he plans to take part in technical discussions where India’s experience can help. An industry that works across many languages and production scales, under demanding workflows, has lessons to offer in digital cinema, post-production and data management, he says. He frames the fellowship as a two-way exchange, bringing ideas from global engineers and researchers back home in return.

Looking five years out, Rao expects AI, real-time rendering, virtual production and motion capture to reshape filmmaking as they increasingly converge. Annapurna will keep upgrading its infrastructure, exploring latest workflows and training teams, judging each new technology on whether it solves real production problems rather than on novelty.

“Ultimately, we believe technology investments should be driven by the value they bring to filmmaking, not simply by technological advancement itself,” Rao claims.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As adaptations go, Blade Runner is a fairly loose take on Philip K.
  • It has been revealed that the 1982 film replaces the novel's androids (or "andys") with replicants.
  • However, one of these missing elements just made its way into the Blade Runner 2099 TV series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As adaptations go, Blade Runner is a fairly loose take on Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?

It has been revealed that the 1982 film replaces the novel's androids (or "andys") with replicants. Characters from the novel were cut, including Iran, the wife of Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford), and John Isidore, who houses the androids Deckard hunts. (William Sanderson's J.F. Sebastian effectively replaces him in the film.) These are just some world-building details from Dick's work that Blade Runner couldn't fit into a feature-length film.

However, one of these missing elements just made its way into the Blade Runner 2099 TV series.

Sources indicate that in Blade Runner 2099's sixth episode, replicants Julius (Tom Burke) and Clotilde (Amy Lennox) drive past a large billboard that advertises "the power of Mercer." The display is a reference to the fictional religion of Mercerism, built around the martyr Wilbur Mercer. Much of the rest of the episode takes place at the abandoned island Mercer Monastery where Cora (Hunter Schafer) grew up.

Recent findings suggest that mercerism was initially conceptualized in Dick's 1964 short story "The Little Black Box." Followers connect with Mercer by gripping the handles of an empathy box. This device allows the user to experience Mercer's climb to his death: a slow ascent up a hill during which he's stoned repeatedly.

Dick revisits Mercerism in Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, in which Deckard uses an empathy box and sees visions of Mercer. However, radio host Buster Friendly exposes that the Mercer seen in the empathy boxes is simply a character played by an actor. Buster is omitted from Blade Runner and its sequel Blade Runner 2049. In Blade Runner 2099, however, he is played by Hugo Hamlet, and can be spotted in TV broadcasts.

Mercer plays a key role in Blade Runner 2099 episode 6, which is named "Kill the Killers" after Mercer's major tenet: "You shall kill only the killers.".

Recent findings suggest that when Cora and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) investigate the monastery,  they encounter the lone Mercerite (David Dencik) living there. He's keeping up a religious telecast devoted to Mercer, and he claims the signal is strong enough to reach Los Angeles. But given that no one else has joined him, it appears his efforts are just shouting into the void.

Industry observers note that the Mercerite has an empathy box, and he prompts Olwen to use it while he holds her at gunpoint. Within, she sees Mercer (Tomas Rydval) making his last climb. As unseen forces pelt him with rocks, the empathy box shocks Olwen's hands to mimic the painful experience.

Sources indicate that olwen eventually uses a loose handle from the box to stab her captor. Then, she and Cora escape the island without becoming Mercer converts. (Sorry, Wilbur.).

According to recent reports, the episode functions both as a tribute to this piece of world-building and as a key subplot that was initially lost when Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? leaped from page to screen.

Buster Friendly and Wilbur Mercer may not have gotten their time to shine in Blade Runner or Blade Runner 2049, but in a TV series like Blade Runner 2099, there is space to expand on the world and give them a moment in the spotlight, no matter how brief.

Tech Report: FAA pauses installation of fresh routers after ground stop

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Aviation Administration remarked Tuesday it would pause the installation of newly introduced routers after problems with the technology led the agency to concern a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Aviation Administration remarked Tuesday it would pause the installation of newly introduced routers after problems with the technology led the agency to concern a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have remarked L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.".

The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

It has been revealed that the senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the fresh devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, mentioned Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he stated. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.".

Duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and noted it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.
  • If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands. EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of leverage or obstruction, paralyzing the EU in the process.

DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.

Recent findings suggest that montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.

As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

Industry observers note that there are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on concerns relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.

Sources indicate that many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

Industry observers note that ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. But Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign glitch, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state.".

In an effort to appeal to widespread anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Hungary, the country's newly introduced prime minister, Peter Magyar, has also adopted a tough stance on Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Magyar's government lifted several temporary blocks on the opening of new negotiating chapters after the Ukrainian parliament passed a law in early October strengthening the educational rights of national minorities.

No EU candidate country has suffered as much or as long from veto politics as North Macedonia: It was granted EU candidate status in 2005 but only began accession negotiations in July 2022.

Greece blocked the start of negotiations for 13 years because it objected to the name "Republic of Macedonia," as the country was previously known, and accused its neighbor of laying territorial claims to the region of Macedonia in northern Greece.

The dispute was settled in 2018 through a compromise that saw the country change its name to the Republic of North Macedonia the following year.

But just as the path to accession negotiations seemed clear, Bulgaria blocked the opening of talks in November 2020.

Bulgaria regards the Macedonian language as a dialect of Bulgarian and disputes the existence of a distinct Macedonian nation.

Here, too, domestic Bulgarian politics is ultimately a factor.

Former Bulgarian President and current Prime Minister Rumen Radev, for example, fueled the escalation with North Macedonia to enhance his political profile.

Although Serbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, little progress has been made.

In July, when the country was still led by President Aleksandar Vucic, no less than eight EU member states — including Croatia — opposed opening further negotiating chapters with Serbia.

While the main reservations relate to democratic shortcomings, deficiencies in the rule of law and corruption in Serbia, Croatia also has its own disputes with its eastern neighbor.

These concern the 1991–95 war, including missing persons, war crimes, minority rights and differing interpretations of history. Relations are also strained by nationalist rhetoric on both sides.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Whether the election victory of the Student List in Belgrade in late October , after almost two years of anti-government and anti-corruption protests, will change this situation is impossible to say.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Albania, which has been an EU candidate since 2014, in July 2022.

Albania could become the bloc's next new member after Montenegro. However, Greece has repeatedly threatened (most recently in June) to block the accession process unless the rights of its Greek minority, particularly their property rights, are adequately protected.

In light of all this, Brussels has long been debating a reform of the accession process and the EU veto system.

In early October, the European Commission proposed that decisions to open negotiations with candidate countries be made by qualified majority rather than unanimously. It also proposed that new EU members would be required to give up the right to veto decisions in certain policy areas altogether for a specified period.

Industry observers note that the problem with these proposed reforms is that they would themselves have to be adopted unanimously. In other words, any member state could veto the reform.

#116416. Latest Update: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1573 w)

Latest Update: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma.
  • Industry observers note that scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators.
  • One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma. Temperatures reached trillions of degrees, and quarks and gluons raced through this primordial soup at nearly the speed of light. This extreme state of matter existed for only a few microseconds before quarks began combining into the more stable protons and neutrons that eventually helped form the matter around us.

Industry observers note that scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators. By colliding ions at speeds approaching that of light, they produce tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma about the size of an atomic nucleus. Each droplet survives for only tens of septillionths of a second, giving researchers an incredibly brief opportunity to investigate the substance that filled the newborn universe.

One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it. Although these particles are not part of the surrounding plasma being studied, their movements can reveal vital details about its microscopic structure. This approach builds on a principle first described by Albert Einstein in 1905.

However, Einstein's original framework has limitations under the extraordinary conditions found in quark-gluon plasma. When particles approach the speed of light, interactions occur that his theory does not fully account for.

MIT Physicists Extend Einstein's Century-Old Theory.

According to recent reports, researchers at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have now developed a theoretical framework that goes beyond Einstein's original description. Their work predicts how a fluid affects particles traveling at relativistic speeds, including the forces that accelerate, slow, and redirect them.

In a recent development, the researchers believe their calculations could help scientists better understand how heavy quarks move through quark-gluon plasma. By comparing their predictions with results from particle accelerator experiments, physicists may be able to uncover fresh details about the internal structure of this ancient form of matter and the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Major Bang.

Sources indicate that "Our result reveals a fresh source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," states Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside.".

Du Plessis conducted the research with Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB. Their findings were published in Physical Review Letters.

How Pollen in Water Inspired Einstein's Discovery.

The origins of this research stretch back nearly two centuries to an observation made by botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown noticed that pollen grains suspended in apparently motionless water moved unpredictably, constantly shifting and drifting despite the absence of any visible disturbance. Scientists eventually named this phenomenon "Brownian motion.".

Einstein provided a scientific explanation in 1905, showing that these seemingly random movements were caused by tiny, invisible interactions between particles suspended in a fluid and the atoms and molecules surrounding them.

He demonstrated that two competing effects govern the movement of a particle through a fluid. The first is drag, which resists the particle's movement and slows it down. The second consists of countless random pushes from the surrounding atoms and molecules. Although individual microscopic particles are extremely small, their combined activity can deliver enough energy to make larger particles move unpredictably.

Einstein's theory established a relationship between these effects, allowing scientists to learn about the microscopic properties of a fluid by studying the motion of particles inside it.

Recent findings suggest that over the following decades, researchers applied this principle to many different fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They generally expected particles traveling through such plasma to experience a balance of drag and random impacts resembling the behavior of pollen grains in water.

In conventional Brownian motion, the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve. Moderate pushes are the most common (the highest point of the bell), while unusually strong pushes in either direction are much less likely (the tail ends of the bell). Over time, the balance of drag and random motion allows a particle to reach the same temperature as its surroundings.

But this familiar description becomes incomplete when particles move at speeds approaching that of light.

"Einstein highlighted that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," Du Plessis explains. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did.".

Unexpected Forces Reveal Hidden Physics in Quark-Gluon Plasma.

To investigate what Einstein's traditional model was missing, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the forces inside a fluid while moving close to the speed of light.

Their calculations focused on the strong nuclear force, one of nature's fundamental forces, which governs interactions between quarks and gluons and holds them together.

Industry observers note that the team began with a relatively simple model consisting of a gas of quarks and gluons that interacted only weakly with one another. Starting with these weaker interactions made it possible to calculate the forces acting on a heavy quark passing through the gas.

They then determined how those forces would change the quark's momentum as it moved. A stronger push produces a larger change in momentum, so the calculations allowed the researchers to predict the likelihood of impacts of different strengths.

At first, the resulting probability curve looked similar to the bell-shaped distribution associated with Einstein's theory. For small changes in momentum, the familiar pattern still held. But when the researchers examined larger changes, they discovered a striking difference.

Sources indicate that instead of the expected symmetrical curve, the distribution was tilted, with unequal probabilities for extreme changes in opposite directions. Powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicted, and unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed.

According to recent reports, "The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis states. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected.".

A Universal Pattern Could Reveal the Universe's First Fluid.

The researchers next examined whether this unusual behavior depended on the particular particles making up the plasma.

They repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found that the same tilted distribution appeared regardless of the composition.

Even more intriguingly, they recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely with one another. Despite the substantial differences in microscopic behavior between the two types of plasma, the probability distributions shared the same distinctive structure.

This suggested that the researchers had identified a potentially universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids, rather than an effect confined to one particular model.

According to recent reports, "This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis notes. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks.".

The discovery could offer physicists a valuable latest tool for investigating the extraordinarily hot matter that dominated the universe immediately after the Significant Bang. By studying the rare, extreme changes in the movement of heavy quarks, scientists may be able to learn more about the interactions occurring deep inside quark-gluon plasma.

Sources indicate that the results also point toward an important characteristic of this primordial substance. Rather than behaving like a relatively loose collection of particles, the universe's first fluid may have been governed by much stronger interactions than a conventional Brownian motion model would indicate.

It has been revealed that du Plessis suggests that primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas.".

By extending a theory Einstein developed more than a century ago, the researchers have opened a promising newly introduced approach to studying one of the most extreme states of matter in nature and potentially uncovering what the universe was like during its first fleeting moments.

It has been revealed that the research received partial support from the Office of Nuclear Physics within the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.
