Tech Report: Microdrama Revenue to Hit $20 Billion in 2026, but Profits Outside China Remain Thin, Media Partners Asia Report Finds

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global microdrama revenue will climb 24% to $20 billion in 2026, but outside China the business has yet to prove it can make reliable money, according to upcoming research from Media Partners Asia.
  • It has been revealed that the Asia-focused research and advisory firm’s second annual study of the sector, “The Microdrama Economy 2026,” projects the market will reach $32 billion by 2031, on annual growth of 9.8%.
  • Recent findings suggest that china still dominates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global microdrama revenue will climb 24% to $20 billion in 2026, but outside China the business has yet to prove it can make reliable money, according to upcoming research from Media Partners Asia.

It has been revealed that the Asia-focused research and advisory firm’s second annual study of the sector, “The Microdrama Economy 2026,” projects the market will reach $32 billion by 2031, on annual growth of 9.8%. MPA’s figures measure spending by viewers, advertisers and brands before app stores and payment processors take their cut. Outside China, they count only dedicated microdrama apps and their web storefronts, not general social media feeds. Related Stories 'Focker-in-Law' Review: Ariana Grande Sporadically Livens Up a Tired Comedy Retread 'Way of the Warrior Kid' Review: Chris Pratt Pulls Too Much Focus in a Conflicted Family Film.

Recent findings suggest that china still dominates. The country will generate $15.2 billion this year, or 76% of the global total, after revenue jumped 90% in 2025. MPA expects growth there to cool to 6.7% annually as viewing levels off, taking Chinese revenue to $21 billion by 2031. The firm’s China figure is narrower than the National Radio and Television Administration’s RMB100 billion ($15 billion) estimate for 2025, which also counts producer outlays on AI models and platform investment.

Sources indicate that free, ad-supported viewing overtook paid viewing in China in 2025. Advertising will make up 69% of the country’s microdrama revenue this year and 79% by 2031. ByteDance, which operates Hongguo and Douyin, takes 56% of Chinese revenue, and ByteDance, Tencent and Kuaishou together command 82%.

In a recent development, dedicated apps outside China will earn $4.87 billion in 2026, a third more than last year, with MPA forecasting $11 billion by 2031 on annual growth of 17.7%. The U.S. remains the biggest single market at $1.71 billion, though that is 2% lower than in 2025. Asia-Pacific excluding China, at $1.44 billion, is set to overtake the U.S. in 2029.

It has been revealed that india, at $322 million, now outranks Japan and Korea as the biggest market in Asia after China. It is also the fastest-growing, with revenue more than tripling this year. Local players Kuku TV and Story TV both roughly tripled their takings, and JioStar launched its microdrama service Tadka on JioHotstar in April. India is the only big market where local platforms lead, selling cheap subscriptions that bypass app-store billing. JioStar’s existing streaming audience has reduced its need to pay for new users, and the company is now turning to retention and growing ad revenue.

Revenue is concentrated. ReelShort, DramaBox–GoodShort, Kunlun and NetShort together generate 65% of the total outside China, and each is either owned or financed from China. DramaBox and GoodShort announced a merger on Oct. 31, the first such deal among the sector’s top players, partly so the two would stop outbidding one another for advertising. Fox, Versant and NBCUniversal are among the U.S. media companies that have bought minority stakes in the sector, while India’s and Korea’s biggest local platforms are gearing up to go public.

In a recent development, some homegrown companies take on the Chinese-owned apps directly, among them Korea’s Vigloo and Fuji TV’s FOD Short in Japan. MPA sees their edge in what the Chinese apps don’t have: built-in audiences, homegrown IP and talent, and a way to bill viewers without payment cards. Japanese and Korean broadcasters, studios and telcos mostly work as producers. Across Southeast Asia, telcos have sold heavily discounted passes to build reach, though MPA noted it is unclear whether these bring in fresh paying customers or simply shift existing ones to a cheaper channel.

Industry observers note that tikTok sits on all sides of the market. It sells advertising to the apps, carries their series and competes with them through its free app PineDrama. In Southeast Asia, ByteDance is repeating its China playbook, building audiences with free, ad-funded apps before cashing in. MPA expects TikTok to become a major player in the U.S. and Southeast Asia alike by 2031. YouTube stays open to creators and studios, while Meta mainly serves as the place where apps find upcoming users. Even so, MPA doesn’t expect free platforms to push out the paid apps, which control the IP and the billing relationship with paying customers.

It has been revealed that profits are the sticking point. For each dollar of revenue generated outside China, 56 cents goes to marketing and another 18 cents to app stores and payment processors. In a typical month, just one in 12 consumers or so pays anything. The two largest groups each bring in more than $1 billion a year, yet DramaBox posted a 3.2% net margin in fiscal 2025. ReelShort lost $12 million in 2025 before swinging to a profit of roughly $8 million in the January-March quarter of 2026.

It has been revealed that “Demand for microdrama is established in every major market, but outside China this is still an emerging business, and it has yet to show that it can earn a durable profit,” stated Vivek Couto, CEO and executive director of Media Partners Asia. “The leading apps spend more than half of their revenue to acquire viewers, and most of those viewers do not pay. Consolidation has begun, and China has already moved to free, advertising-funded viewing. The companies that endure will be those that retain their viewers, bill them directly and invest in titles worth returning to.”.

AI is reshaping supply far faster than demand. By MPA’s count, new titles listed on non-China apps will surge from around 100,000 in 2025 to 440,000 this year, with the AI-generated share climbing from 15% to 75%. Each listing represents a single title in a single language on a single app, so a series that runs in multiple languages or across multiple apps indicates up more than once. Producing a title with AI costs roughly 10% of what a Los Angeles shoot would.

Sources indicate that audiences have been slower to switch. Live-action titles hold most of the top 50 spots on five of the six non-China platforms MPA tracks. In China, about nine in 10 titles released in 2026 are AI-made, but they bring in just 20% of the year’s revenue.

“What decides a platform’s economics is how many of its titles earn back the marketing spent on them,” mentioned Myat Pan Phyu, MPA’s lead analyst for microdrama and vertical video. “That favors companies with established IP, stars and audiences of their own, which is why local broadcasters, studios and telecom operators matter to the next phase.”.

Industry observers note that payments may shift the math. Apple and Google process 65% of the revenue earned outside China, though legal rulings and fresh legislation in the U.S., Japan and Korea have cleared the way for web payments. Direct billing can lift margins, although the savings depend on each market’s fees and payment route. MPA expects payments made outside the app stores, including through India’s UPI system, to deliver roughly half of the growth outside China in 2027.

The detonation follows concerns that cooling winter temperatures or attempts to chemically neutralize the materials could lead to an unexpected, uncontrolled explosion.

According to recent reports, "In challenging circumstances such as this, you want the nation's best on the field. That is precisely why you call on NASA, putting our airborne and space-based sensors and some of the brightest scientific minds in the country to work," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman remarked in an online statement.

Industry observers note that to support this detonation, NASA deployed three research aircraft: a P-3 Orion, a Gulfstream III from NASA's Langley Research Center and a B200 from NASA Ames. The agency is also monitoring the situation using its TEMPO (Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution) instrument which is mounted and orbiting Earth on a commercial satellite.

"Working alongside our partners across the federal government, NASA is utilizing its advanced scientific instruments and expertise to collect environmental and atmospheric data to inform the broader federal response," NASA stated.

The environmental monitoring using TEMPO is especially notable as the materials to be detonated include lead azide and other toxic components that are causing not just environmental worries, but significant local concern over possible health repercussions. This concern is severe enough that, following detonation, officials are encouraging local residents to stay indoors with the doors and windows closed for 24-28 hours.

While this planned detonation has unsurprisingly caused concern among locals and nationwide, Isaacman has urged the public not to mischaracterize the event as something larger.

"Even if it's hyperbole, it is irresponsible to characterize this as a 'Chernobyl event,'" he said online in response to someone likening the event to the infamous nuclear accident.

It has been revealed that "When there is no reactor and there are no fission products. This is a controlled detonation of aging explosive material and is being handled in the most responsible way possible.".

#116411. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • According to recent reports, new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
  • The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

According to recent reports, new research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

According to recent reports, chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

It has been revealed that despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising latest questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

In a recent development, "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

In a recent development, the researchers also examined how rapidly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

Recent findings suggest that finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred indicates. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The upcoming findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

Sources indicate that the research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

  • The move capped a chaotic 18 hours in which the team unveiled it was benching the 42-year-old future Hall of Famer for backup Mason Rudolph ahead of Friday’s visit from Denver.
  • Rodgers responded by taking an excused absence from the club, then used the unexpected time off to go on McAfee and repeatedly call the 62-year-old McCarthy’s mental state into question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aaron Rodgers came to Pittsburgh in a Chevy.

He left it sitting atop a flamethrower.

The Pittsburgh Steelers cut the four-time NFL Most Valuable Player on Wednesday, shortly after he torched Steelers coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on ESPN’s The Pat McAfee Show.

The move capped a chaotic 18 hours in which the team unveiled it was benching the 42-year-old future Hall of Famer for backup Mason Rudolph ahead of Friday’s visit from Denver. Related Stories Business Tony Romo Lands Post-CBS Gig With Betting App Betr as "Chief Predictions Officer" (Exclusive) TV Tom Jackson, Denver Broncos' All-Pro Linebacker and ESPN Analyst, Dies at 75.

Rodgers responded by taking an excused absence from the club, then used the unexpected time off to go on McAfee and repeatedly call the 62-year-old McCarthy’s mental state into question.

Rodgers told McAfee he found out about the surprise decision while on the phone with teammates, including tight end Pat Freiermuth.

It was just the start of a blistering offensive from Rodgers, who painted McCarthy — whom he played under during a long successful run in Green Bay earlier in their careers — as a leader woefully out of touch.

He described a quarterback meeting last Wednesday with McCarthy arriving late, sat down “and within 10 minutes began snoring,” woke up and nodded off again minutes later, then eventually “walks out of the room like nothing happened.” Rodgers also remarked McCarthy missed an offensive meeting Thursday, missed a walkthrough Friday and a morning meeting Saturday while not holding a team meeting that night.

“And then comes to Sunday, when obviously we struggled and the product wasn’t great,” Rodgers noted, adding that McCarthy broke up the halftime locker room meeting by saying “1-2-3 Packers.”.

Rodgers said he felt it was the right thing to bring up the complications to McCarthy as a longtime league star instead of putting it on others with fewer years, shaky roster positions or those who “haven’t made $400 million dollars in the NFL.”.

In a recent development, “Me? I don’t care, what are you going to do to me?” Rodgers stated. “Like I said, you’re going to release me? Cool. You’re going to deflect this thing and make it that you were trying to bench me and that I’m at home contemplating whether or not I’m going to accept a benching? Couldn’t be farther from the truth.

According to recent reports, “That word never came up in our meetings. What came up was: sleeping, habits, gameplan, understanding what we’re doing, being able to call a play, being able to call a game without the game sheet.”.

The scene played out bizarrely during Rodgers’ extended appearance on the show in which he has been an occasional contributor. McCarthy waded through a throng of assembled reporters in the lobby — most of them huddled over their phones listening to Rodgers — after practice ended.

Minutes later in a subdued locker room, the Steelers left to pick up the pieces declined to get into specifics about Rodgers’ accusations but didn’t dismiss them either.

Asked if he’s confident McCarthy can lead the team going forward, Freiermuth responded with a simple “I’m confident” but little else.

Wide receiver Marquez Valdes-Scantling, who played alongside Rodgers and under McCarthy as a rookie in Green Bay in 2018, acknowledged there was general frustration about the team’s recent performance but allowed “I didn’t think it was this.”.

Rodgers has already said this will be his last season. Now it’s fair to wonder if he’ll reach the end of it — in Pittsburgh anyway — after McCarthy turned to Rudolph, a longtime backup, with the Steelers (6-4) trying to snap out of a two-game funk before it’s too late.

In a recent development, there’s little precedent for sitting a future Hall of Famer and Super Bowl winner midseason. Johnny Unitas, playing out his final days in a Chargers uniform, got benched for rookie Dan Fouts after four games in 1973.

Joe Namath never played again after throwing four picks in a loss to Chicago during a late-career cameo for the Los Angeles Rams a month into the 1977 season.

More recently, Denver replaced Peyton Manning with Brock Osweiler midway through 2015 even with the club sitting at 7-2. Manning returned in the season finale and then served as a game manager in the playoffs as the Broncos’ dominant defense led the franchise to its third Super Bowl victory.

Manning walked off the field with the Lombardi Trophy in tow in his final game.

While the Steelers are right now in playoff position, their next three games are against AFC West-leading Denver, surging Houston, and AFC South leader Jacksonville. While they can probably withstand one loss or maybe even two, three could be catastrophic.

Enter Rudolph, who rescued Pittsburgh’s season and briefly earned folk hero status in 2023 by coming off the bench in December and authoring a surge to a playoff berth.

That didn’t stop the Steelers from moving on from him immediately, bringing in Russell Wilson and Justin Fields in 2024 and then Rodgers in 2025, a move designed to help Pittsburgh end a postseason victory drought that’s nearing a decade.

Recent findings suggest that rodgers’ first year ended with a blowout playoff loss at home to the Texans. His future seemed uncertain until the Steelers hired McCarthy to replace Mike Tomlin in January, a job Rodgers played a hand in helping McCarthy land, though how substantial a hand is up for debate.

In a recent development, not that it mattered in the end. Rodgers opted to make one last run at a championship while reuniting with the coach he won a Super Bowl with in early 2011.

According to recent reports, A storybook ending on the field seems remote. Pittsburgh is a woeful 2-4 on the road, where it figures to be when the playoffs start if the Steelers can’t track down Cincinnati in the race for the AFC North title.

And the team’s Jekyll/Hyde play in general has offered little tangible proof that it is a legitimate threat to have an extended postseason stay.

It has been revealed that rodgers’ play has mirrored that of his team. He tossed three touchdowns in three consecutive weeks, even outdueling Cincinnati star Joe Burrow in a victory over the Bengals in late September.

Yet he’s struggled to make an impact of late, often checking the ball down to running backs Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle or taking sacks behind an inconsistent offensive line when trying to push the ball down the field to a receiving group that has underperformed, particularly two-time Pro Bowler DK Metcalf.

Rodgers averaged just 0.5 air yards per attempt in the first half last week against Philadelphia, the lowest since ESPN began measuring the stat in 2006.

It has been revealed that what happens next to a player who has always leaned into doing things on his terms at all times is unclear. Pittsburgh was supposed to be his third and final NFL stop.

He seemed content on Tuesday, spending time in the locker room trading jokes with Rudolph and longtime defensive tackle Cam Heyward after addressing reporters.

Barely eight hours later, Rodgers was no longer the starter. Shortly after that, he was no longer a Steeler, the latest and perhaps final twist in a journey that will end with him getting a gold jacket at the Pro Football Hall of Fame, even if this ends up being an inglorious off-ramp for all involved.

AP Pro Football Writer Rob Maaddi and AP Sports Writer Aaron Beard contributed to this story.

U2 Salutes Dolly Parton With Recreation of Their ‘Torn’ Duet in NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton as part of its halftime performance Wednesday night at the NFL‘s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game.
  • It has been revealed that U2 did not attempt to cram as many songs into their brief performance as other superstars have during halftime performances, getting in four.
  • Dolly Forever <3 U2 pays tribute to Dolly Parton with “Torn” during their halftime performance pic.twitter.com/c4CfeoQiXi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic.

Recent findings suggest that U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton as part of its halftime performance Wednesday night at the NFL‘s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game. The “duet” between a live Bono and a recording of Parton from last summer was the centerpiece of a highly promoted 10-minute set between halves of the contest between the Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers, streamed exclusively on Netflix.

It has been revealed that U2 did not attempt to cram as many songs into their brief performance as other superstars have during halftime performances, getting in four. The band opened with an abridged “Sunday Bloody Sunday” and ended with “”Pride (in the Name of Love)” and Where the Streets Have No Name” — only squeezing in one song from their latest album, the Parton duet, “Torn,” with images of Dolly projected onto three huge curtains that dropped around their stage at the 50-yard line.

Dolly Forever <3 U2 pays tribute to Dolly Parton with “Torn” during their halftime performance pic.twitter.com/c4CfeoQiXi.

In a recent development, about a hundred extras took part in the performances — forming not a marching band, but a marching choir. U2 was also joined by the Womack Sisters, a vocal trio that has just been nominated for best new artist at the Grammys.

Sources indicate that the dancers first appeared as part of “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” which included an interpolation of the Supremes’ “Stop in the Name of Love,” rendered as something more somber, as performed by the Womack Sisters, to better fit in with U2’s theme of civil war. Bono repeated the “torn” part of that early ’80s anthem as a segue into the song “Torn,” as he and the spectral Parton harmonized on the recent song about a family at war. After one last look at Dolly, the curtains dropped to the field and the dancers formed three concentric circles around the band’s platform, repeating the familiar strains of of “Where the Streets Have No Name” and then “Pride (in the Name of Love)” as the Womacks joined U2 on stage.

It has been revealed that U2 performs 'Where The Streets Have No Name' at the NFL Thanksgiving Eve halftime show. pic.twitter.com/dXhj4KQbPk.

Sources indicate that technically, five U2 songs made their way into the set, as eagle-eyed or -eared U2 fans were able to catch a bit of “American Obituary” during “Sunday Bloody Sunday.” The song, which appeared on a recent EP from the band, references the killing by ICE of Renee Good. Related Stories U2 Gets On Its Boots for First All-New Full-Length Record in Nine Years, 'Carnaval de Luz,' With More Callbacks to Band's '90s Peaks Than '80s Glories: Album Review Geese’s Soaring Live Show Lives Up to the Hype, With Fearless Improvisations and Boundless Energy: Concert Review.

The four key songs were just condensed enough that U2’s members were actually able to use part of their allotted 10 minutes walking to the stage at the beginning and walking back out through the assembled marchers at the end, in casual yet dramatic fashion.

WHAT A PERFORMANCEU2 performs '(Pride) In The Name of Love' with The Womack Sisters at the NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show pic.twitter.com/ZBzEZ1SUIt.

Some political subtext relevant to the times was seen by at least a small subset of fans in that assemblage of material, although it hardly would have been evident to less hardcore fans or strictly NFL-oriented viewers. That was evident in connecting “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” about the Irish conflicts, with the “American Obituary” snippet. Then, bringing in the Parton song might have been a no-brainer anyway, as her part on the duet was said to be the last studio recording ever made by the superstar before she died in August. But beyond that, the theme of the tune has been described as reflecting the kinds of squabbles that occur among families when relatives get together for Thanksgiving and air their political differences around the dinner table, with Parton playing the role of the mother who wants everyone to mend what drives them apart.

Although this was the NFL’s first such Thanksgiving Eve halftime show, it is in a very recent tradition of superstars doing holiday halftimes; the previous ones have just been for Christmas. On Dec. 24, 2024, a Baltimore/Houston game featured a performance by the latter city’s hometown favorite, in the “Beyoncé Bowl.” For Christmas Day 2025, the NFL enlisted Snoop Dogg for a “Holiday Halftime Party.” No intends have been revealed as of yet for a Christmas halftime extravaganza from the NFL.

U2’s camp reportedly approached the NFL themselves with the idea of doing a Thanksgiving halftime show — obviously timed to capitalize not just on families gathered around the TV before a holiday, but, from U2’s perspective, following closely on the heels of the Nov. 13 release of “Carnaval de Luz,” the band’s first album of new material in nine years. The album debuted at No. 4 on the latest Billboard 200 chart.

It was U2’s third tango with the NFL, albeit its first in two decades. The Irish band famously did the Super Bowl halftime show in 2002, with an emphasis on honoring the victims of 9/11. In 2006, the group performed in celebration of the opening of the Louisiana Superdome after Hurricane Katrina.

The group has kept up a heavy cycle of broadcast and streaming promotions before and since the new album release, including a surprise opening to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony at L.A.’s Peacock Theatre on Nov. 14, which is being edited into a special to be broadcast Dec. 8 on ABC.

Sources indicate that on Monday, U2 announced the itinerary for a 15-date tour of North American stadiums in 2027, on top of already announced shows in Central America and Europe. The tour has them returning to the site of their NFL performance, SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., presumably for much longer performances, on oct. 1-2, 2027.

Ukraine's bid for NATO membership and more air defense remains controversial

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

💡 Key Takeaways

  • "Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It took a while for the video call to connect. When Volodymyr Zelenskyy finally greeted the delegates in Berlin, applause broke out. The Ukrainian president appealed to the gathered parliamentarians from 32 NATO member states to keep supporting his country, especially against the massive aerial bombardment from Russia.

"Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us. And of course, our number one priority is air defense," Zelenskyy told the delegates. His country urgently needs more Patriot and other comprehensive anti-air attack systems. "And your countries have them. Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust. And we say this openly. Please help us with this.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that zelenskyy renewed his call for his country to join the NATO military alliance. That matter is not for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, which was gathered for its 72nd annual meeting in Berlin, to decide. But it was important to the Ukrainian president to reiterate his request.

Industry observers note that after the war ends, Ukraine needs strong security guarantees and NATO could ensure those. "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" Zelenskyy asked, arguing: "Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Cheaper to put in place? And more reliable when it comes to actually protecting security?".

There is conflict among NATO members about the possibility of admitting Ukraine. The alliance has affirmed multiple times that the path to membership stands open to Ukraine — however, in the long term rather than the near future. This is primarily because of the ongoing war and the possible assistance obligations of other NATO countries for Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia.

In a recent development, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rejected the Ukrainian demands at the summit, which for the first time in 26 years was held in Berlin. Ukraine had entry prospects; however, NATO members at the moment lack unanimity on this problem. NATO alone decides who becomes a member. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance," Rutte stated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz advocated for Ukraine to receive security guarantees similar to what NATO members have, in the instance of a possible ceasefire. In retrospect, it was clear "what a mistake it was not to follow the American suggestion back in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine as a member," Merz stated at a joint press conference following a meeting with Rutte.

Whether or not a NATO entry for Ukraine could be part of negotiations with Russia is another question, according to Rutte. He approved of current US efforts to bring about peace talks, and how Europe was closely consulting with Ukraine and the US for a unified position. "But it is also to test now whether Putin is willing to play ball, and then these issues might come up again.".

The Russian invasion of Ukraine has led to NATO arming itself on a massive scale. Members have committed to raising their countries' defense spending to 5% of their gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.

Rutte warned that all the allies needed a credible path to get there, "and ideally, they get there sooner than 2035." In addition, he stated weapons production among member states needed to further increase because "right now, demand still far exceeds the supply.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that the contribution by Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces to NATO was explained by Carsten Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier. For example, the massive increase in military spending: "Our defense budget has tripled since 2021. The goal is to achieve the 5% target, which was set at the summit in The Hague, well before 2035." In the coming year, Germany's defense budget has risen to more than €139 billion ($151 billion).

The Bundeswehr was further developing into a "constantly modernized, effective and innovative army, Breuer noted. Also, a much larger one than before. "To reach our current capability goals we are expanding the Bundeswehr to a total of 460,000 soldiers by the mid-2030s," the German chief of defense said. Of those, 200,000 are to be reservists. "This is like walking a tightrope because we must find the right balance between growth and operational readiness.".

Following his speech, Breuer answered questions from the delegates who highlighted keen interest in the developments. The discussion was a preview of Breuer's latest post: He has been voted in as the new chair of the NATO Military Committee and will move to the alliance's headquarters in Brussels mid-next year. Then he will become the principal military advisor to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. "I take this election as a sign of recognition that Germany has now accepted its responsibility as well as its role in security policy," Breuer said.

This article was originally written in German.

DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, how did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions?
  • Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA.
  • According to recent reports, the research was led by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, how did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

According to recent reports, the research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists.

According to recent reports, one of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An crucial difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage.

The results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an important advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," remarked Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule.".

This finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

Upcoming Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection.

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

The team established a new set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," said Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team proposal to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

Recent findings suggest that A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

Industry observers note that "We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins.".

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

One of the biggest shopping events of the year is finally here: Black Friday.

In a recent development, early Black Friday deals started rolling in weeks ago, but now we're well into the official sales. Yes, instead of standing in a cold line at 4 a.m. the day after Thanksgiving, we get to shop online under cozy blankets while watching Christmas movies.

Recent findings suggest that since the deals between retailers can feel overwhelming, it's good to head into the mega-sale event with a initiative. From knowing when sales from retailers like Amazon and Best Buy start to knowing which products will likely go on sale to preparing your own shopping list, we've got you covered on everything you need to know to shop Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Industry observers note that this year, Black Friday falls on Nov. 27, but that date isn't all that key these days. Almost every major retailers has already started official Black Friday sales. We expect to see some special deals drop on Nov. 27, but if you're looking to shop Black Friday sales, it's your time to shine.

Absolutely yes. The mega-retailer's sale kicked off Thursday, Nov. 19 — more info on the full date range of the sale is below. Expect deals on everything from the year's top tech to home essentials. Naturally, Amazon's devices also get markdowns across the board. So far, the retailer has teased the following:.

Save up to 45% on Amazon's 2024 Kindle Colorsoft, 55-inch Ember Artline TV, and 55-inch Ember Mini LED-Series TV.

Save up to 50% on select headphones and speakers from Sony, Beats, JBL, Marshall, and Sonos.

Save up to 40% on select Ninja appliances, including the Creami, Foodi, and Slushi.

Save up to 40% on select iRobot and Bissell floorcare.

Amazon: Amazon's Black Friday sale runs from Thursday, Nov. 19 to Nov. 30, offering 12 consecutive days of deals. Each day of the sale will feature "Today's Massive Deals," where select products will be on sale for up to 60% off, except for on Black Friday and Cyber Monday proper. One batch of deals will go live at 3 a.m. ET, while another will go on sale at 11 a.m. ET.

Best Buy: Black Friday at Best Buy starts on Nov. 19, and runs through Saturday, Nov. 28. Its Cyber Monday sale runs from Nov. 29 to Nov. 30, with a Cyber Week sale that extends savings from Dec. 1 to Dec. 6. Total and Plus members of the My Best Buy program are also eligible to earn double points on their purchases from Nov. 19 to Dec. 6.

In a recent development, walmart: Walmart has three major sale events throughout November: the early Black Friday sale from Nov. 12 to Nov. 15, the Black Friday sale from Nov. 23 to Nov. 29 (with deals online only from Nov. 23 to Nov. 26), and the online-only Cyber Monday sale from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2.

Industry observers note that target: Target's first Early Black Friday sale kicked off Nov. 5 to Nov. 7. From Nov. 1 to Dec. 24, Target's Deal of the Day offer kicks off, featuring new deals every day. Every weekend after Nov. 7, the retailer will also drop new limited-time holiday offers.

It has been revealed that considering prices went up this year on pretty much Apple devices except for AirPods, Black Friday will be the time to pick up fresh Apple devices. The slightly longer answer: the best place to pick up Apple products during Black Friday sales will be at retailers like Amazon, Walmart, or Best Buy, which often duke it out to see who will drop a MacBook or pair of AirPods to the record-low price first (or, more impressively, keep it in stock the longest). Already in the lead-up, MacBooks are $250 off, and the AirPods Pro 3 are $100 off.

Target has great Black Friday deals if you're looking for toys, Lego sets, Christmas decor, books, or small kitchen appliances. Target's Deal of the Day offers extra savings on hot items, and you can preview upcoming deals several days before they happen, giving shoppers time to set a reminder.

While Black Friday brings many of the best prices of the year, it's not the end-all, be-all for every product out there. According to Google-analyzed holiday trends, fancy cookware and suitcases hit their lowest prices in late December, while tech like TVs and gaming consoles are likely to hit their lowest prices during Black Friday and Cyber Week (with the latter seeing one final dip right before Christmas).

Recent findings suggest that there can be some variance from category to category, so we recommend keeping track of Mashable's deals coverage. Our team has been covering Black Friday (and deals in general) for nearly a decade, so we can tell your firsthand whether or not a product is worth grabbing during the height of sales.

With Black Friday proper bringing some of the lowest prices, what deals are worth shopping now? It's an especially relevant question in 2026, a year that saw many historic price increases across everything from laptops to Kindles. In other words, shopping smart has never been a smarter decision, which is why we've gathered some of the best early Black Friday savings so far.

It has been revealed that the more apt question is what doesn't go on sale during Black Friday. That's to say, if there's a product you're looking to grab on sale, whether that be a new TV or paper towels, Black Friday is the time to do it.

Beyond the deals we have listed above, we expect to see more savings on MacBooks, Windows laptops, video games and consoles, robot vacuums, regular stick vacuums, drones, trading cards, books, board games, and power tools. Some deals do linger through the week, and some Cyber Monday sales (such as Walmart's) are scheduled to extend beyond Cyber Monday proper. And as Target's deal-of-the-day sale demonstrates, there are almost always Black Friday-worthy sales through essentially Christmas. That stated, for the best shot at scoring massive savings (and for catching a deal while it's still available), shopping during Black Friday weekend is typically a good rule of thumb.

Amazon and Walmart don't offer any price matching policy. Best Buy's Holiday Price Match Guarantee offers price matches against itself through Jan. 15, 2027 on products purchased from Oct. 30 to Dec. 31. Target used to offer price matching against other retailers during the holidays, but now its policy resembles Best Buy's: Target shoppers who made a purchase on or after Nov. 1 in person or online can request a price match if they spot a drop on or before Dec. 24.

  • He gradually climbed the ranks to first assistant director, eventually trading B-movies for some of the biggest studio productions around, including Guillermo del Toro’s Pacific Rim and Gareth Edwards’ Godzilla.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Filmmakers often thrive on controlled chaos. Alex Gayner has spent his career orchestrating that madness.

Long before producing The Mosquito Bowl for Peter Berg, Gayner cut his teeth doing odd jobs on ’90s direct-to-video actioners — the kind of movies you’d stumble across on a pay-cable channel at 1 AM during a bout of insomnia. Then, a second assistant director was let go before lunch, and Gayner found himself promoted on the spot. It was an unlikely break that set the course for the rest of his career.

He gradually climbed the ranks to first assistant director, eventually trading B-movies for some of the biggest studio productions around, including Guillermo del Toro’s Pacific Rim and Gareth Edwards’ Godzilla. He also developed a reputation as a closer, overseeing reshoots for Suicide Squad (2016), Birds of Prey, Zero Dark Thirty and Mulan, among others. Related Stories TV 'Beef' Creator Lee Sung Jin Launches Production Company, Aims Ali Wong Limited Series Movies Ray Nicholson Levels Up With 'The Mosquito Bowl': "I'm Always Battling for Legitimacy".

Another turning point arrived in the late 2010s, when the native New Yorker decided to pivot to producing. If the first AD is the on-set quarterback who executes the plays on the field, then Gayner wanted to become a full-time offensive coordinator, the person drawing up the plays and mapping out the production behind the scenes.

In a recent development, he credits Nicolas Winding Refn with giving him his significant break as a producer on the 2019 limited series Too Old to Die Young, an opportunity that paved the way for him to produce the first season of Beef and win an Emmy for his work. (Gayner and Refn are now assembling the latter’s long-gestating Maniac Cop reimagining, which recently received approval for a California tax credit.).

Industry observers note that after wrapping Beef, Netflix pointed Gayner toward Berg’s 19th-century Western limited series American Primeval. But first, the two had to bridge the gap between the producer Berg expected and the one Gayner turned out to be.

According to recent reports, “When I met Pete, I don’t think he really knew what kind of producer I was,” Gayner tells The Hollywood Reporter. “Naturally, he didn’t know if I was going to come in to watch the money or try to make the show on soundstages. We had to figure each other out.”.

To keep the football metaphors going, Berg likes to run his sets with a no-huddle offense, frequently calling audibles along the way. He might improvise dialogue, change camera positions or throw out the playbook altogether. Most of all, he has a strict devotion to immersive, practical filmmaking. Fortunately, Gayner has been adapting on the fly ever since that lunchtime promotion more than 30 years ago. He also shares Berg’s preference for capturing as much as possible in camera.

Thus, they quickly got on the same page for American Primeval, setting the stage for two features, The Mosquito Bowl and the highly anticipated Call of Duty video game adaptation.

Industry observers note that “That [adherence to practical] really solidified our relationship as filmmaking partners. He knew I wasn’t afraid to go back to the old-school way of how we learned to do things,” Gayner indicates. “It’s a little uncomfortable to get that realism and that immersive, visceral experience on film, but it’s worth pushing the envelope.”.

According to recent reports, the Mosquito Bowl, based on a novel by Berg’s cousin Buzz Bissinger, chronicles four real-life college football players who enlisted in the U.S. Marine Corps during World War II and played in a fabled 1944 football game known as the Mosquito Bowl alongside 60 other former collegiate players turned soldiers.

Berg and Gayner threw Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis into football crash courses with help from San Francisco 49ers All-Pro running back Christian McCaffrey, the New York Giants and two of the industry’s best on-set football coordinators. Then they dropped the actors into the ocean and jungle of Queensland, Australia, doubling for Japan, while surrounding them with tanks, explosions, flamethrowers and blank gunfire.

According to recent reports, berg wanted to honor one specific character detail that belonged to Nicholson’s Tony Butkovich, the former Purdue University fullback who was drafted in the first round by the NFL’s Cleveland Rams prior to enlistment. Bissinger wrote about how Butkovich sent photos home of himself with a parrot on his shoulder, so Gayner received the unenviable task of tracking down what would become the one-and-only available parrot on the island continent. But the bird was still young, and its wings had to be clipped to prevent catastrophe during filming.

After months of planning and training, cameras finally rolled on Nicholson and the supposedly grounded parrot. Within seconds, the parrot flew off into the 100-foot-tall trees. Its four wranglers panicked, as did the rest of the stunned cast and crew. Gayner, meanwhile, tried to counter Berg’s fatalism with optimism.

Industry observers note that “Pete looked at me and said, ‘I know exactly what’s going to happen. The headline of every entertainment paper in L.A. is going to be, “Peter Berg Kills Parrot During Filming of The Mosquito Bowl.”’ And I said, ‘No, Pete, we’re going to find the parrot.’”.

Hours later, they managed to retrieve the parrot from a tree and tie a string to its leg as an added precaution until they got the necessary shots. The trial amounted to roughly ten seconds of footage in the final cut, but it’s a stark reminder of how much labor goes into even the briefest moments on screen.

“We can control actors, special effects and stunts. But when the only parrot in Australia that’s available for our movie flies away, you’re stuck,” Gayner states. “We didn’t want to use a CG parrot. We’d made that commitment.”.

Below, in a conversation with THR, Gayner elaborates on training two British actors and a Swedish actor to play a sport they’d never played before, let alone understood.

Recent findings suggest that your filmography is overwhelming. You’ve seen some things, haven’t you?

Recent findings suggest that (Laughs.) I’ve seen a few things, yeah. I’ve been around the block. I’ve gone from tiny little things to significant giant things — and everything in between.

In a recent development, I can only imagine the war stories you must have, especially as first assistant director. That’s widely considered the most stressful job on set. First ADs are often regarded as the quarterback to the director’s head coach. Did you have any kind of support group with your fellow first ADs?

Not really, because first ADs never work with other first ADs. You can talk to each other, share experiences and discuss your approaches to working with directors, but you never really get to spend time with them, especially on a movie set, unless there’s a first and second unit. Everybody has such different styles. But it is a stressful job. It’s a heavy-lifting job.

Industry observers note that I started making films in Hollywood when I was 20 years old, and I worked for a very low-budget film company that made straight-to-video action movies. They filmed one movie every three weeks. So we would do 18-day shoots — three consecutive six-day weeks — with the exact same crew. We’d wrap a movie on a Friday, and then we’d start a upcoming movie on a Monday. You’d get the script midway through one movie, and everybody would just roll onto the next film. I did that for three years, and I made 30 films in three years.

I did everything from driving the grip truck to learning how to load film, because we were still shooting film at the time, to being a boom person and working with the grips and the electric. So it really was my film school, and it taught me so much about what everybody does on a film set. Then I just happened to fall into the AD department because a second AD got let go. At lunch, they were like, “Alright, you’re now the second 2nd.” And I was like, “Okay, I’ll figure out how to do that.” Eventually, that happened with the [first] AD.

Why do you think these assistant director roles fit you so well?

Industry observers note that I have a knack for communicating with all the departments and rallying everybody to have a common vision. And as I started to become a first AD on smaller movies before eventually doing some second-unit action sequences and working my way up to the bigger studio films, I made it less stressful for myself. I really understood what everybody was up against and what everybody was doing. I didn’t want to live under that constant pressure of only being focused on, How are we going to make our day? How are we going to get the schedule done? We have to just keep going.

That is part of the job, but really, I’m a filmmaker. I want to participate creatively in supporting the story and the characters. And as a first AD, if you can figure out how to do your job and motivate the crew — while working in a respectful environment with a couple hundred people, keeping them on the same page and being a good creative partner to the director, the producer and the studio — it takes a lot of the pressure off. You’re not being this machine butting up against an artist trying to birth something that’s in their brain.

So, as a first AD, I was always a creative first, and I figured out how to translate that into the schedule, the days, the shot lists and the time that the DP had to light. Integrating myself as a creative partner to everybody made it less stressful and more enjoyable.

Another pattern in your work is that you tend to assistant-direct a lot of additional photography. Examples include: Suicide Squad, Birds of Prey, Zero Dark Thirty, Mulan and Total Recall. That’s a fraught period of time since the production is spending the last of its money, and there’s a lot riding on the additions and/or revisions. Was there a reason why your number kept getting called for reshoots? Are you the Winston Wolf of reshoots?

Industry observers note that (Laughs.) I don’t really know the answer. Part of it was schedule and circumstance. Another part of it was word of mouth. I really took pride in what I did as a first AD, and I’m a very even, mild-mannered first AD. There are some who are not. Everybody has their own style, but I always was very balanced and very calm in the pocket, so to speak, to go back to your quarterback reference. So I think that reputation just got around town.

Also, if a director’s usual first AD wasn’t available for reshoots, I tended to be on the short list to be called. It was very flattering. It was a really great way to build relationships with other directors without having to commit a year or two to the overall process, and it expanded my résumé quite a bit.

You’d produced here and there prior to 2023, but did your Emmy for producing Beef season one lead you to produce full-time? It looks like you stopped assistant-directing that same year.

According to recent reports, I’d been going back and forth before producing Beef. The last movie I AD’d was Spiderhead with Joe Kosinski during COVID. It was a very hard transition. I’d worked so long to be successful as an AD, and then I looked in the mirror and went, “Alright, I’m going to stop doing this and make the transition to producer.” With a family and a mortgage, it was a substantial commitment to step into a latest role, essentially starting at the bottom. But I knew that it was the natural next step, something I had to do and really wanted to do. The project that got me really confident as a producer was a limited series called Too Old to Die Young that Nicolas Winding Refn directed.

Big fan. Every time I see Nell Tiger Free, I remind her how haunting her beach scene with Miles Teller is.

I absolutely remember that day. We went up to the [Mugu] rock at the end of Malibu, right on the turn there. It was a wild show, and I loved making it. Nick originally called me to AD the series, and I turned him down because I was really committed to producing. But he kept calling me and calling me. And I noted, “Nick, look, I really appreciate it, but I have to stick to this. I have to make this transition. This is what I’m going to do.” In 2017, limited series really weren’t that big a thing yet, and Amazon, under Roy Price, was also still finding its legs. This was long before Jen Salke came in.

Sources indicate that then Nick stated, “I’ll tell you what, I’m going to direct this entire series by myself, which I’ve never done before. If you AD the first episode of the show for me, I’d love for you to produce the series. Once you get me on my feet, then you can produce the rest of the episodes. I just need you to prep for me and help me with casting and finding locations.”.

Recent findings suggest that so we figured out what would work for him and what would work for me, and we made a deal. I AD’d the first three weeks or so, and then I stepped off the set. Other ADs then came in, and I produced the rest of the show. Nick wrote the series with Ed Brubaker, and besides directing all the episodes, he was editing every night. So he was at it seven days a week, 20 hours a day.

It was a fantastic experience and one of the most creative things I’ve ever been a part of. It was such a specific vision that he had. We shot most of it in L.A. over a hundred days. It was a very small-budget show, and we stretched every dollar. That was really the beginning of producing for me.

Do you think Maniac Cop is ever going to happen?

I’m as sure as I can be. It just qualified for the California Tax Credit. It got approved. He’s making it as a film instead of a series. We tried to make it as a series for HBO. We were very close to making it, but once COVID hit, it was just impossible to make that kind of show at the time.

You wrapped Beef season one in 2022. In 2023, you EP’d American Primeval for Pete Berg. Did you hit it off to such a degree that he wanted you to be his boots-on-the-ground producer and UPM for The Mosquito Bowl?

American Primeval was a very complicated show to make out in the elements for a hundred-plus days. I was asked to come in as a non-writing EP. Pete and I had never worked together. I’d never even met him. I had previously worked with the other executive producer, Eric Newman, and I had a longstanding relationship with a lot of people at Netflix.

Sources indicate that when I met Pete, I don’t think he really knew what kind of producer I was. He’s worked with a lot of the same people over the years, and he has this very raw, immersive, visceral vision of whatever he’s making. So, naturally, he didn’t know if I was going to come in to watch the money or try to make the show on soundstages. We had to figure each other out.

In a recent development, but as soon as we hit the ground in New Mexico, he learned that I have the same desire to make films and television as practically as he does. There are definitely benefits to going on stage and shooting blue screen for certain pieces, but for a huge sequence at the end that takes place on top of a snowy mountain, there was talk of going to a quarry-type setting and making fake snow in a very controlled environment. As soon as I started talking creatively with Pete about it, I knew there was no way this was going to work for what he was trying to do visually and what Mark L. Smith wrote.

My first reaction and suggestion to that proposed plan was, “I don’t want to do that. I want to gather a lean crew with as little gear as possible, and climb up a mountain in the real snow. We can build a shack and do it for real, while having access and keeping everybody as safe and comfortable as humanly possible.” To fabricate all that in the Latest Mexico summer and then add visual effects, it would’ve felt too different. Paper snow doesn’t react to horses the same way as real snow, and that went for every element of that sequence.

So that [adherence to practical filmmaking] really solidified our relationship as filmmaking partners. He knew I wasn’t afraid to go back to the old-school way of how we learned to do things. It’s a little uncomfortable to get that realism and that immersive, visceral experience on film, but it’s worth pushing the envelope.

Pete is known for having a very vocal, energetic and off-the-cuff directing style. He’ll throw out alternate dialogue mid-take without cutting. How did you adapt your own process to his “no-huddle” manner of shooting a movie?

Recent findings suggest that I didn’t have to adapt that much. Working with Pete as a producer, it’s like creating an action-packed play. He’s very improvisational. If something comes to mind on set, he goes for it. Being a First AD for so many different kinds of directors, as well as shooting additional photography, really served me as a producer. I learned how to step into a preexisting structure, whether for a couple of scenes or a whole sequence, and adapt to a crew that’s already been through battle together. As a producer, I try to be as responsible for the active environment I’m creating as I am for the story.

Pete especially likes a 360-degree environment, and that’s how I approach every project. There’s no cheating. You can’t go out to a location with all your trucks lined up behind you and say, “Okay, you can only look west.” That 360 approach really slimmed everything down, allowing us to be nimble and giving Pete the freedom to say, “Okay, I want to turn around and look the opposite way.” It helped us discover some magic on American Primeval and The Mosquito Bowl. Organic pieces of the puzzle fell into place. The actors appreciated it, too.

Mosquito Bowl has numerous war and football sequences, which must have been a logistical nightmare. You weren’t the First AD on this set, but that experience must have also served you well here.

100 percent. Every challenging project I’ve produced has been made better by my experience and the tools I gained as a first AD. The Mosquito Bowl wasn’t a logistical nightmare, but it was very challenging logistically. There were so many challenges to figure out on a daily basis that I had to use every tool in my toolbox.

When Pete started writing and talking about The Mosquito Bowl while we were shooting American Primeval, we agreed that if we were going to make a war movie, we had to do something different. So many amazing World War II films have already been made. We had to take responsibility for trying to capture even 0.1 percent of what these soldiers went through emotionally. Obviously, we would never compare what we do as filmmakers to what any soldier experienced in war, but we had to deliver something immersive, violent and shocking for the audience while remaining true to what really happened.

Recent findings suggest that that meant putting the actors in the ocean instead of in a water tank or a pool and using real explosions and blank gunfire instead of visual effects. We had to find running tanks and develop hundred-foot flamethrowers. As a producer, I was never going to let “it’s impossible” come out of my mouth. There was always going to be a way to make it as real as possible, and that became our mission statement from the beginning.

Industry observers note that with every person we interviewed and every department we approached about joining The Mosquito Bowl, we said, “This is how we want to do it. We want to make this as real as possible. Can you do this? Are you up for it? And what are your ideas to help us get there?”.

Did San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey consult you guys as far as how to train the actors to look like capable football players in just four weeks?

He absolutely did. Christian McCaffrey helped us build the foundation for the actors to become football players. Pete, who’s friendly with Christian, gave him a call once we had Nicholas Galatzine, Bill Skarsgård, Tom Francis and Ray Nicholson on board. Christian is a beast. He’s one of the most amazing football players there is, and he’s such a gracious guy. He does so much work with veterans, and he’s involved with a nonprofit, so he was immediately willing to donate his time. He was even coming back from an injury at the time, but two days after Pete called him, he was on the field in Westlake with Ray, running plays, teaching him moves and consulting as a running back. Additionally, we sent Tom Francis to the Upcoming York Giants because he was doing Sunset Boulevard on Broadway, so he got to train with them.

Sources indicate that we had two Brits, a Swede and one American, and with Ray being the American, he was the only one who had ever really played football. He played high school football and knew a lot about the game, but Nick, Tom and Bill didn’t know much about it. So they worked tirelessly with our football coordinators, Mike Fisher and Don Powers, who have worked on a lot of football movies. They came down to Australia and ran a four-week camp with the actors, bringing in a ton of Aussie rules football and rugby players, as well as a few college football players from the States to fill in at quarterback.

For all the football and battle sequences, ten seconds of a parrot interacting with Ray’s character was the task that put you through your paces the most?

Sources indicate that (Laughs.) That put Pete through his paces more than anything else on the movie. I don’t know about myself. Every single day, my brain was working at a hundred miles an hour trying to solve problems. Birds and animals in Australia are different from those in other parts of the world. You have some of the deadliest snakes and spiders, as well as bull sharks. Everywhere you go, you have to be aware of nature’s pitfalls. So finding movie animals there was difficult, and Australia doesn’t have every breed you might find in North America or elsewhere.

Industry observers note that ray’s character, Tony Butkovich, really had a parrot as a pet during World War II. That was based on real information. But finding a movie-trained parrot that looked the way we wanted was nearly impossible. We worked with animal wranglers who eventually found one, but it was very young. They had to train it so we could feed it.

They also clipped its swings so it wouldn’t fly away. We had to shoot the scene within a specific window before the parrot got old enough to learn how to fly. So we were up against the deadline of the parrot instinctively knowing how to fly. We also shot the whole movie in continuity, so our first AD, Andrew Ward, had to figure out how to fit the scene into that window.

It has been revealed that there had been months of logistical planning and training, and Ray had to understand what he could and couldn’t do with it. Eventually, the day came when we had to work with the parrot. We were in the jungle, surrounded by smoke. Everyone was carrying guns and wearing all this gear, but everything had to be silent and still.

Gosh, all this for ten seconds of footage.

Yeah, when Ray sat down to do the scene, the set had to be cleared. Pete couldn’t call action, and nobody could say a word. The animal wranglers put the parrot down next to Ray and made hand signals for the cameras to start rolling. Ray started feeding the parrot, and within two seconds, it flew off into the jungle. (Laughs.) The parrot that wasn’t supposed to be able to fly with its clipped wings disappeared up into the trees.

The animal wranglers freaked out, and we all had to stop and look up. We were looking for a tiny parrot in the Australian jungle, surrounded by hundred-foot trees and dense foliage. The animal wranglers then crawled through the jungle, making parrot noises and trying to call it back.

Pete looked at me and mentioned, “I know exactly what’s going to happen. The headline of every entertainment paper in L.A is going to be, ‘Peter Berg Kills Parrot During Filming of The Mosquito Bowl.’” And I said, “No, Pete, we’re going to find the parrot.” So the search went on for hours, and the animal wranglers stacked ladders and held pool cues with baskets on the ends. Eventually, the parrot came back and we got the shots, but it was one of the most stressful ordeals.

Recent findings suggest that we can control actors, special effects and stunts. We can have that kind of input. But when the only parrot in Australia that’s available for our movie flies away, you’re stuck. We didn’t want to use a CG parrot. We’d made that commitment.

You just proved why I’m endlessly fascinated by behind-the-scenes stories. Of all the projects you’ve been a part of, which one deserves the I Play Rocky treatment?

It’s between American Primeval and Too Old to Die Young, but it’s hard to pick one or the other because they’re very different.

American Primeval was logistically the hardest project I’ve ever produced and made. We did it for real in the Fresh Mexico desert through winter, spring, summer and fall, with no cover sets and no place to go, with horses and 1800s footwear and clothing, a writers’ strike and a SAG strike. Taylor Kitsch, our lead actor, even broke his foot, and Betty Gilpin, our lead actress, got pregnant during the strikes before having to come back to finish the show. We went from shooting in one winter season with the heaviest snow in New Mexico to finishing the show the next winter season, and it was New Mexico’s warmest winter with no snow.

Recent findings suggest that too Old to Die Young was the most eccentric creative experience I’ve ever produced. Nick shot 10-minute-long takes where the camera didn’t move. We drove around Hollywood at three in the morning with John Hawkes and Miles Teller. They drove a police car by themselves up the 405 while I was in the backseat with a camera in my hand. A CHP officer followed us and allowed us to do that night after night. It was the most surreal experience.

***The Mosquito Bowl is now streaming on Netflix.
