📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the sixth and final episode of “South Park” Season 29, South America has once again been hit with major power outages — but this time it’s serious, considering “Grand Theft Auto VI” has finally been released, which means the residents of the mountain town will stop at nothing to restore their Xboxes and PlayStations and continue playing the long-awaited video game.

Industry observers note that “Damn it, Mayor! We have waited over a decade for this game to come out,” proclaims one angry South American resident at the top of the episode. “Do you have any idea how ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ works? If it shuts up while it’s saving or during a mission, you lose everything.” The issue, though, is that the South American government has made a deal with a group of billionaire weenies, as was introduced in the season’s second episode, who are using the town’s energy to power their data centers. Related Stories 'Jimmy' Review: Cornball James Stewart Biopic Gets the Manner, but Not the Man 'Situations' Review: Greg Vrotsos' Filmmaking Debut Is a Winning, Relatable Throwback.

The town’s politicians have no idea what to do about the glitch, but luckily for them, a group of angry townspeople barge into South American City Hall and proclaim they know who’s behind the outages: the Chinese. More specifically, the outages are the result of Chinese cyberattacks. Relieved, the town’s politicians let them believe this is the case — “Yes, you figured it out. It’s definitely cyber attacks by the Chinese” — as they begin to search for a Chinese spy who must be living in South America.

Recent findings suggest that but Butters has known the billionaires were to blame since the beginning, and confides in Stan, Kyle and Cartman. Oh, and a zombified Kenny (who got blown up by an e-bike during the season’s premiere) also makes a few appearances. Turns out, Kenny’s spirit can’t move on until the group figures out what’s going on and exposes all the corruption in South America — great timing for them, as they’ve all learned about the data centers and are ready to make a change. The gang takes this revelation to City Hall, where the politicians explain how it all began “with those damn e-bikes” and fear that the group of kids is going to blow their secret deal with the billionaires.

Industry observers note that but it wasn’t an e-bike that killed Kenny, claims a still shrunken Randy who barges into City Hall. “We all did. We all share in the blame equally… When they changed the name of our town, we let it change us. We used force, took bribes, looked the other way, because we let them change South Park.”.

In the end, the mayor of South American addresses the town and owns up to her mistakes — kind of.

“I owe you all an apology. Since the town changed its name, I’ve taken bribes. I’ve looked the other way, and I did make a deal with billionaires,” she says. “But I’ve learned that even though we must build data centers because there is a very real threat from the Chinese in the AI arms race, we can’t let that change who we are.”.

And so, the billionaire weenies help the town “do something we should have done a long time ago”: shoot Mr. Kim into space and out of South America. And with that, another season of “South Park” (and the first season with the new name of “South America”) comes to a close.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this past election, Americans across the country rejected data centers, voting to restrict new projects in their communities. As voters push back against data centers, a new study out of Harvard reveals startling revelations about the severity of the pollution they create.

Pollution from data centers is three times higher than previously estimated, according to a upcoming study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

The study examined 403 "hyperscale" data centers and found that emissions from these facilities were underestimated. In fact, the lead author Gianluca Guidi believes that their research only provides a "floor estimate." When factoring in the thousands of data centers across the country, many of which were not included in the study, the energy use is likely much higher.

The study found that the largest data centers in the U.S. use as much energy in a single year as the state of Michigan does. Carbon emissions from these data centers surpassed those of entire countries.

Sources indicate that researchers found that 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. during the study period came from data centers. A single data center included in the study consumed as much energy as 30,000 homes on average. Booking Holdings is bringing together two of its business-to-business travel operations in a new division it hopes will be transformational, betting that a larger, coordinated partner platform can generate growth as artificial intelligence changes how travelers discover and book trips.

In a recent development, the latest enterprise unit, dubbed Booking Partner Division, will combine Booking.com Strategic Partnerships with Rocket Travel by Agoda, and is set to begin operating in January. Agoda CEO Omri Morgenshtern will lead the unit, which aims to help businesses such as banks, airlines and online travel companies sell trips or build branded experiences for their customers.

"We realize that if we focus our efforts both on the product side, but also on the go-to-market side, then we can potentially grow faster and serve better partners," Morgenshtern told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

He said existing partners will find upcoming and better products, which will also help grow the partner base.

Industry observers note that the move gives Booking a single organization to coordinate technology, travel supply and commercial expertise across business relationships. The company notes partners will be able to use its global supply and technology through white-label platforms, integrated applications, branded solutions and hotel-chain rate distribution.

The portfolio includes more than 4.7 million properties, 33 million accommodation listings, more than 500 airlines and more than 200 car rental providers, according to the organization.

Competitor Expedia Group has seen notable growth by prioritizing its enterprise efforts, including a strategy debuted in 2022 to make its technology platform available to business partners looking to add travel to their own offerings.

From 2018 to 2023, Expedia’s business-to-business revenue grew at a 16% compound annual rate, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, for the division grew at a 28% rate, the tech giant stated in 2024.

It has been revealed that in 2025, Expedia’s B2B revenue rose 18% to $4.8 billion, and its segment adjusted EBITDA increased 22% to $1.26 billion. Those figures represented about a third of Expedia’s total revenue and more than a third of its adjusted EBITDA for the full year.

Morgenshtern declined to say how much the new division is expected to contribute to Booking Holdings' overall revenue and profit, but he said the opportunity for growth is immense, estimating the total addressable market at $2 trillion.

Online travel agencies have been pressured this year as investors scrutinize how AI will change the way customers search for and then book their travel.

Companies that offer lodging, experiences and other travel and leisure are grappling with how to stay visible if AI tools become the newly introduced starting point for planning and reservations.

Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro remarked on the tech giant’s earnings call Tuesday that guests already use AI to discover and strategy Disney trips, and that some are using the tools to book.

“Ultimately, we want Disney to show up in those tools,” he mentioned, adding that Disney is exploring ways to let guests make reservations directly from them.

Booking anticipates offering partners AI capabilities that draw on the company's existing travel know-how while minimizing token costs, it said.

Sources indicate that "I see a lot of AI demos," Morgenshtern noted, drawing a distinction between a product that caters to a few customers and one that's scalable and works even when overloaded by travel emergencies. He said he's "super optimistic" about the bespoke product — a vertical agent — that Booking will offer to its partners.

Hera spacecraft gets 1st up-close look at stadium-sized hole punched in asteroid by NASA DART mission

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the Hera spacecraft.
  • NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept.
  • Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the Hera spacecraft.

NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept. 26, 2022, when it slammed into Dimorphos, the small moonlet of the much larger asteroid Didymos. The mission tested if such an impact could be deployed to divert an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Scientists have known for some time that this deflection attempt was successful; the system's orbit around the sun was lengthened by 33 minutes, but the European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera mission rolled out in October 2024 to travel the 120 million miles (194 million kilometers) to the Didymos system to observe the effect of the DART impact in greater detail.

Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically. The impact also appears to have blasted out hundreds of previously unknown boulders that are now circling the binary asteroids.

"Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same," Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said in a statement.

"Much to our surprise, the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width.".

Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, detailed some of the changes to the impacted moonlet seen by the spacecraft: "As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit.

"Another significant surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size.".

It has been revealed that it wasn't all change for Dimorphos. Hera discovered that the boulder fields covering the regions of the moonlet not impacted look just like they did when DART imaged it in 2022.

Hera isn't finished with Didymos and its moonlet. The ESA spacecraft is currently in a rectangular orbit around the asteroid binary system, using its thrusters to maintain a distance of around 18.6 miles (30 kilometers). This allows Hera to continue observing Didymos and Dimorphos.

It has been revealed that hera will soon come to within around 8 miles (13 km) of the asteroids, capturing even more detailed images of the space rocks. Following this, it will deploy two showbox-sized CubeSats, which will get even closer to the asteroids.

Sources indicate that the CubeSat Juventas will use low-frequency radar to probe the interior of Dimorphos, the first time this has ever been done for an asteroid, and will eventually attempt to land on the moonlet to measure its gravity. Meanwhile, the Milani CubeSat will prospect asteroid materials and dust around the Didymos system.

Together, Hera and its CubeSats will more precisely determine the mass of Dimorphos, which, when combined with information about the orbital change of the system, will be crucial in planning missions to deflect threatening asteroids.

Hera's observations were revealed on Wednesday (Nov. 25) at the dinosaur hall of the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, Germany. That location isn't a coincidence: It is a stark reminder of why this planetary defense mission is so notable. Especially if humanity doesn't want to go the way of the dinosaurs, whose rule on Earth ended when an asteroid fell from the sky."Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid impact changed the course of life on Earth. Today, for the first time in history, humanity is validating how to prevent such an event from happening again," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli explained. "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. "By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.".

The German government has presented some grim statistics with regard to misogyny, rape, violence and murder, with reported cases of domestic violence at an all-time high.

At a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig released the latest figures on crimes that specifically target women: whether within families and intimate relationships, in public or online.

In contrast to the statistics pertaining to crime overall, which have remained the same or increased only slightly, reports of crimes against women have increased.

"Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories, people and particularly women and girls, whose lives are severely affected by these acts of violence," said Dobrindt.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In 2025, some 280,000 people were victims of physical abuse in their own homes, a 2.8% increase compared to the previous year. Over 70% of the victims were female. Each hour, 16 women are subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors.

The male victims included boys who had been assaulted by their fathers.

The number of misogynistic hate crimes has also risen dramatically, by almost 50%, to 819 cases.

According to recent reports, "The figures show us what it can mean to be a woman in Germany," remarked Hubig. "It can mean being killed by one's partner or ex-partner. Being a woman can also mean being physically abused by one's partner or ex-partner in one's own home. Being a woman can mean that one's sexual autonomy is brutally disregarded.".

According to the latest findings, both perpetrators and victims are getting younger. In 2025, nearly half of all female victims of sexual offenses were under the age of 18. And the number of incidents of online violence against women and girls rose by 15.7%. This includes the unauthorized sharing of videos and photos, verbal abuse, manipulation of images, threats and online blackmail, as well as cyberstalking.

Because many perpetrators and victims are still in their teens, Prien, who is also minister for education, said the government wanted to focus primarily on schools, which she explained should become places of prevention.

It has been revealed that "Ultimately, we need to bring about a change in people's mindsets, especially those of men. That will be the deciding factor in the end," she noted.

Over the weekend, Justice Minister Hubig had already announced that in future all femicides, the intentional killing of girls and women because of their gender, would be classified as murders. At the moment, such crimes are often classified as manslaughter, for which the penalty is less severe than for murder.

Hubig told German broadcaster ZDF that it was increasingly common that femicides be described as family tragedies or as domestic dramas revolving around jealousy and then classified as manslaughter.

In a recent development, martina Link, the vice president of the Federal Criminal Police Office, was also at the press conference in Berlin. She called for everybody to pay closer attention to the issue, within their own families, neighborhoods or at work.

Recent findings suggest that "Violence against women is not a private matter," she remarked. "Not in our immediate surroundings nor in the digital world.".

She also pointed out that when it came to sexual offenses and domestic violence, only about 5-10% of cases were reported.

A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes.
  • According to recent reports, in a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve vital biological functions.

According to recent reports, in a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation.

One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

Sources indicate that they found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

In a recent development, this research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal key new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

"We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," mentioned Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

Sources indicate that he added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject.".

Gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," remarked Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

He added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine.".

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island.

Jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

It has been revealed that he arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

It has been revealed that today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

Catherine Hardwicke, who helmed 2008’s Twilight, might as well have had a crystal ball on the set of the vampire romance film.

After it was revealed earlier this month that Robert Pattinson — who earned his breakout role as Edward Cullen in the blockbuster franchise — had been tapped as the newly introduced James Bond, fans were quick to point out that Twilight predicted his 007 casting nearly two decades ago.

It has been revealed that at one point in the movie, Eric’s (played by Justin Chon) discusses the prom theme and indicates, “Gambling, tuxedos, and Bond, James Bond,” right before the camera cuts to a smirking Edward, looking suave in a pair of sunglasses. Related Stories Movies Prince Harry Approves of Robert Pattinson's Bond Casting Movies The Time Robert Pattinson Snuck Around Rikers Island (and Why It Could Help Him With James Bond).

In a recent interview on The Kyle Buchanan Show, Hardwicke recalled how that line and scene came about. “You guys have probably seen online where we have that [Twilight] scene where he [Eric] says, ‘Bond, James Bond,’ and then we cut to Rob,” she stated. “That’s the one scene where I was like, ‘Let’s put the sunglasses on that day,’ and he got out of the car and he looked so suave that he inspired the line, ‘Bond, James Bond.’.

It has been revealed that the director added that Chon “kind of ad-libbed it, and it was kind of cool because we did think he looked like James Bond. So I guess we were seeing the future.”.

In a recent development, fast forward to 2026 and Denis Villeneuve, who’s helming the upcoming 007 movie, and producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, obviously thought Pattinson looked like Bond too. The Primetime actor is taking over the iconic role from Daniel Craig, who concluded his run with 2021’s No Time to Die.

Hardwicke also shared her reaction to the news that Pattinson would be going from having “the skin of a killer” to getting his license to kill.

“I almost fell out of my bed,” she quipped about the moment she learned about the casting. “I just didn’t think they were going to choose him because of The Batman and he’s so famous and they like to get the unknown [actor]. So I did almost fall out of the bed, and that is the same bed that Rob and Kristen [Stewart, who played Bella Swan in Twilight] auditioned for the first time and did their kissing scene. So it was kind of bizarre. And he [Pattinson] fell out of the bed when he did the audition and landed on the floor, so it was kind of cool.”.

According to recent reports, hardwicke continued to praise The Batman actor’s talents, adding, “He’s intense and interesting and has got a lot of stuff going on in there. He’s weird and he’s original. He does not fit the mold. He’s not afraid to say crazy shit, that’s what I love about it.”.

It has been revealed that when The Hollywood Reporter caught up with Hardwicke in 2023, ahead of the 15th anniversary of the first Twilight film, she opened up about the challenges of finding the right actor for the role of Edward. She said the actors who were initially auditioning “didn’t look like they’d been alive for almost 100 years and all this deep, soulful angst, existential crisis. They did not feel that kind of soulful.”.

However, once Stewart and Pattinson did their chemistry read, the director knew he was the one because she felt “that electricity” between them.
